tomato_early_blight.name: Tomato Early Blight
tomato_early_blight.affected_parts: Foliage, stems, fruit calyx, and mature fruits
tomato_early_blight.symptoms: Characteristic dark brown to black necrotic lesions with concentric circular rings forming a distinctive 'target board' or bullseye pattern. Lower, older leaves show symptoms first, surrounded by chlorotic yellow halos. Severe defoliation occurs, exposing fruits to sunscald. Stem lesions appear collar-rot like on young seedlings.
tomato_early_blight.causes_biology: Fungal pathogen that overwinters as mycelium or conidia in crop debris, solanaceous volunteer plants, and solanaceous weeds. Can also be seed-borne. Conidiophores produce brown beak-shaped conidia that penetrate through stomata, wounds, or direct epidermal penetration.
tomato_early_blight.encouraging_conditions: Warm temperatures between 24°C to 29°C (75°F to 85°F) combined with alternating wet and dry periods. Prolonged dew, frequent rainfall, overhead irrigation, and dense canopy humidity favor rapid sporulation.
tomato_early_blight.spread_mechanism: Conidia are readily dispersed by wind currents, splashing rain drops, mechanical equipment, and workers touching wet foliage.
tomato_early_blight.prevention_methods: Implement minimum 3-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops. Use certified disease-free seeds and transplants. Apply mulch to create a physical barrier preventing soil-splashing conidia. Prune lower 12 inches of suckers to promote air circulation.
tomato_early_blight.cultural_control: Eliminate crop residue immediately post-harvest via deep plowing or composting away from fields. Stake and trellis vines to elevate foliage. Irrigate exclusively using drip systems during early morning.
tomato_early_blight.biological_control: Preventative biofungicides containing Bacillus subtilis (Serenade ASO), Trichoderma harzianum (Rifai strain T-22), or copper octanoate (copper soap). Foliar applications of cold-pressed neem oil (0.5-1%) suppress early conidial germination.
tomato_early_blight.chemical_management: Preventative protectants: Chlorothalonil (1.5-2.0 kg/ha) or Mancozeb 75% WP (2.0-2.5 kg/ha). Curative and systemic options upon initial threshold: Azoxystrobin (250 ml/ha) or Difenoconazole 25% EC (0.5 ml/L) or Boscalid + Pyraclostrobin. Alternate chemical classes to prevent QoI resistance.
tomato_early_blight.ipm_recommendations: Begin regular scouting 3 weeks after transplanting. Calculate Tom-Cast disease forecasting units; spray only when Disease Severity Values (DSV) exceed 15.

potato_late_blight.name: Potato Late Blight
potato_late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked irregular pale green to dark brown lesions that expand aggressively without clear margins. Under high humidity, a delicate white downy mildew-like fungal bloom forms on the underside of leaves at lesion margins. Stems develop dark greasy water-soaked girdling lesions causing lodging. Tubers show shallow granular reddish-brown dry rot that turns into foul secondary bacterial soft rot.
potato_late_blight.causes_biology: Heterothallic Oomycete that primarily overwinters as vegetative mycelium within infected seed tubers, cull piles, and volunteer potato tubers. Produces sporangia that release 8-12 motile biflagellate zoospores in free water.
potato_late_blight.encouraging_conditions: Cool, humid, and rainy weather. Temperatures between 15°C to 20°C (60°F to 68°F) with relative humidity exceeding 90% for at least 10 consecutive hours. Epidemics can destroy entire fields within 7 to 10 days.
potato_late_blight.spread_mechanism: Airborne sporangia can travel tens of kilometers on moist cloud-shielded winds. Zoospores swim through water films on foliage and wash into soil ridges to infect developing tubers.
potato_late_blight.prevention_methods: Plant only certified disease-free seed tubers. Eradicate all cull piles and volunteer potatoes before emergence. Hill soil deeply around potato rows (minimum 10-15 cm cover) to prevent zoospores washing down to tubers.
potato_late_blight.cultural_control: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation. Space rows generously (75-90 cm) aligned with prevailing winds to enhance foliage drying. Terminate vines 2 weeks before harvest (haulm destruction) using diquat or flumioxazin to avoid tuber inoculation during lifting.
potato_late_blight.biological_control: Application of Trichoderma viride and Pseudomonas fluorescens seed treatments can slow early soilborne spread. Phosphorous acid salts (potassium phosphite) boost plant systemically acquired resistance (SAR).
potato_late_blight.chemical_management: Preventative contact protectants: Mancozeb 75 WP (2.5 kg/ha) or Chlorothalonil 75 WP or Copper hydroxide. Curative translaminar/systemic chemistry under active outbreak: Metalaxyl-M + Mancozeb (Ridomil Gold 2.5 kg/ha), Cymoxanil + Mancozeb, Dimethomorph (50% WP at 1 g/L), or Cyazofamid.
potato_late_blight.ipm_recommendations: Deploy BLITECAST or Simphyt predictive decision support systems. Initiate spray programs when accumulated risk hours hit trigger points prior to visible symptoms.

rice_blast.name: Rice Blast (Leaf & Neck Blast)
rice_blast.affected_parts: Leaf blades, leaf collars, culm nodes, and panicle neck node
rice_blast.symptoms: Spindle-shaped or diamond-shaped lesions with pointed ends, gray to ash-white centers, and dark brown to reddish-brown margins on leaf blades. Lesions coalesce causing total leaf drying (blast burn). Neck blast infects the panicle node causing 'rotten neck', causing sterile whiteheads or breaking of panicles before grain filling.
rice_blast.causes_biology: Ascomycete fungus forming melanized appressoria that exert enormous turgor pressure (over 8 MPa) to mechanically rupture the silicified rice cuticle. Overwinters on infected straw, stubble, and seeds.
rice_blast.encouraging_conditions: High relative humidity (>90%), leaf wetness exceeding 12 hours, night temperatures around 20°C to 24°C, overcast skies, and excessive split doses of chemical nitrogen fertilizers.
rice_blast.spread_mechanism: Tremendous quantities of pyriform three-celled conidia released during dew periods and transported through air currents.
rice_blast.prevention_methods: Adopt blast-resistant rice cultivars (e.g., harboring Pi-genes). Treat seed with carbendazim or tricyclazole before soaking. Avoid excessive basal and top-dressed nitrogen fertilizer; apply silica amendments (calcium silicate) to reinforce leaf cuticle.
rice_blast.cultural_control: Maintain proper water depth in paddy fields (blast is much more severe in aerobic or water-stressed drought conditions). Burn or deeply incorporate infected stubble. Avoid late-season planting.
rice_blast.biological_control: Bio-priming seeds with Pseudomonas fluorescens (strain Pf1 at 10 g/kg seed) and foliar spraying at 2.5 kg/ha at booting stage. Spraying Bacillus velezensis extracts.
rice_blast.chemical_management: Tricyclazole 75% WP (0.6 g/L or 300-400 g/ha) applied at late tillering and boot leaf emergence. Isoprothiolane 40% EC (1.5 ml/L), Kasugamycin 3% SL (1.5-2.0 ml/L), or Azoxystrobin 18.2% + Difenoconazole 11.4% SC.
rice_blast.ipm_recommendations: Continuous field monitoring at tillering and panicle emergence. Threshold: 1-2 spindle spots per leaf across 5% of tillers. Immediate prophylactic neck blast spray at 5-10% flowering.

grape_powdery_mildew.name: Grape Powdery Mildew (Oidium)
grape_powdery_mildew.affected_parts: Berries, leaves, green shoots, and rachis
grape_powdery_mildew.symptoms: White to ash-gray powdery web-like patches on leaves and young green canes. Infected berries turn dull, leathery, and develop webbed russeting. As berry skin loses elasticity, expanding fruit splits open, exposing seeds to secondary sour bunch rot and botrytis.
grape_powdery_mildew.causes_biology: Obligate biotrophic parasite that overwinters as cleistothecia (chasmothecia) in bark crevices or as dormant mycelium within dormant buds (flag shoots).
grape_powdery_mildew.encouraging_conditions: Warm, shaded canopies with temperatures between 20°C and 27°C. Unlike downy mildew, powdery mildew does NOT require free water droplets; in fact, free rainfall washes away spores. High humidity promotes conidial germination.
grape_powdery_mildew.spread_mechanism: Conidia are wind-blown through the vineyard canopy from primary flag shoots and burst chasmothecia.
grape_powdery_mildew.prevention_methods: Intensive canopy management: shoot thinning, shoot positioning, and leaf removal around fruiting zones (leaf pulling) to maximize direct sunlight and airflow.
grape_powdery_mildew.cultural_control: Prune out infected dormant shoots showing red-brown cane scarring. Avoid excessive vigor from excessive irrigation or nitrogen.
grape_powdery_mildew.biological_control: Wettable sulfur sprays (3-5 kg/ha) provide excellent bio-compatible prevention. Ampelomyces quisqualis (hyperparasitic fungus), potassium bicarbonate (Armicarb), or paraffinic horticultural oils (Stylet-Oil at 1-2%).
grape_powdery_mildew.chemical_management: Triazoles: Tebuconazole 25.9% EC (1 ml/L) or Penconazole or Myclobutanil. SDHI fungicides (Boscalid, Fluopyram) or Strobilurins (Kresoxim-methyl, Trifloxystrobin). Rotate FRAC groups (FRAC 3, 7, 11) to avoid resistance.
grape_powdery_mildew.ipm_recommendations: Begin prophylactic protection at 10-15 cm shoot growth, continuing through bloom and bunch closure when berries develop ontogenic resistance.

grape_downy_mildew.name: Grape Downy Mildew
grape_downy_mildew.affected_parts: Leaves, tendrils, young shoots, and immature grape clusters
grape_downy_mildew.symptoms: Yellowish, translucent oily lesions ('oil spots') on the upper surface of foliage. On the corresponding lower leaf surface, dense white cottony downy sporulation develops during overnight humidity. Infected flower clusters wither, turn brown, and drop. Mature infected berries turn grayish-blue and mummify.
grape_downy_mildew.causes_biology: Obligate oomycete overwintering as thick-walled sexual oospores in fallen vineyard leaf litter.
grape_downy_mildew.encouraging_conditions: The classic '10-10-10 rule': 10 mm of rainfall, temperature at least 10°C, and shoot growth at least 10 cm (4 inches). Overnight relative humidity >95% induces profuse sporangial release.
grape_downy_mildew.spread_mechanism: Rain-splash transports soilborne oospores up to lower canopy leaves. Secondary cycles spread rapidly by airborne sporangia.
grape_downy_mildew.prevention_methods: Maintain weed-free under-vine strips to eliminate moisture reservoirs. Till fallen leaves into soil to bury overwintered oospores. Optimize row drainage.
grape_downy_mildew.cultural_control: Canopy suckering, hedging, and leaf removal around clusters to allow quick drying after rains.
grape_downy_mildew.biological_control: Copper-based organic fungicides (Bordeaux mixture: copper sulfate + hydrated lime at 1:1:100 ratio). Laminarin (algal oligosaccharide plant defense elicitor).
grape_downy_mildew.chemical_management: Preventative protectants: Mancozeb 75 WP, Folpet, Captan, or Copper hydroxide. Curative translaminars: Metalaxyl, Dimethomorph, Cymoxanil, Mandipropamid (Revus), or Fosetyl-Aluminium.
grape_downy_mildew.ipm_recommendations: Monitor weather forecasts for rain events during pre-bloom and post-bloom. Apply systemic protection immediately prior to predicted rain.

wheat_leaf_rust.name: Wheat Leaf Rust (Brown Rust)
wheat_leaf_rust.scientific_name: Puccinia triticina (syn. Puccinia recondita f. sp. tritici)
wheat_leaf_rust.symptoms: Small, scattered, circular to oval blister-like pustules (uredinia) on the upper surface of leaves. Pustules erupt to shed thousands of powdery reddish-brown to orange spores. Later in the season, dark brownish-black teliospores develop.
wheat_leaf_rust.causes_biology: Macrocyclic, heteroecious rust fungus requiring an alternate host (such as Thalictrum speciosissimum or Isopyrum) for sexual reproduction, but propagating asexually via repeat urediniospore cycles on wheat crops.
wheat_leaf_rust.encouraging_conditions: Moderate temperatures between 15°C and 22°C (59°F to 72°F) accompanied by dew formation or free water on foliage for at least 6-8 hours.
wheat_leaf_rust.spread_mechanism: Urediniospores are extremely resilient and can be transported hundreds of kilometers across continental air corridors ('Puccinia pathway').
wheat_leaf_rust.prevention_methods: Cultivate rust-resistant wheat varieties carrying effective Lr genes (e.g., Lr34, Lr67 adult plant resistance genes). Destroy volunteer wheat plants (green bridge) between crop seasons.
wheat_leaf_rust.cultural_control: Sow wheat at recommended optimum planting dates; late sowing exposes wheat to peak spore showers during warm spring weather. Balanced potassium fertilization.
wheat_leaf_rust.biological_control: Seed biopriming with Bacillus amyloliquefaciens and foliar sprays of bio-formulations containing Cladosporium uredinicola hyperparasites.
wheat_leaf_rust.chemical_management: Foliar triazole applications: Propiconazole 25% EC (500 ml/ha) or Tebuconazole 250 EC (1.0 L/ha) or Pyraclostrobin + Epoxiconazole at flag leaf emergence (Zadoks scale GS 39-55).
wheat_leaf_rust.ipm_recommendations: Protect the top two leaves (flag leaf and F-1), which contribute over 70% of photosynthates to final grain yield. Spray when rust pustules reach 1-5% severity on lower canopy.

apple_anthracnose.name: Apple Anthracnose & Bitter Rot
apple_anthracnose.affected_parts: Fruit, twigs, branches, and trunk bark
apple_anthracnose.symptoms: On fruit: sunken, circular brown lesions with concentric circles of salmon-pink to orange gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) under humid conditions. On branches: elongated, sunken cankers with raised calloused margins ('fiddle-string' cankers) where bark splits and exposes inner wood fibers.
apple_anthracnose.causes_biology: Fungal spores survive in bark cankers and mummified fruits left hanging in orchards from previous seasons.
apple_anthracnose.encouraging_conditions: Warm and rainy weather with temperatures around 25°C to 30°C. Long wetness periods during summer pre-harvest weeks.
apple_anthracnose.spread_mechanism: Conidia are embedded in a gelatinous matrix spread by rain splash and wind-driven precipitation.
apple_anthracnose.prevention_methods: Prune out and burn all dead wood, branch cankers, and mummified fruits during winter dormancy. Sanitize pruning shears between cuts.
apple_anthracnose.cultural_control: Improve orchard air drainage; avoid overhead irrigation. Harvest fruit promptly upon maturity and cool immediately.
apple_anthracnose.biological_control: Post-harvest or late-season bio-coatings with Bacillus subtilis or Aureobasidium pullulans (Blossom Protect).
apple_anthracnose.chemical_management: Captan 50 WP (2.5-3.0 kg/ha) or Mancozeb applied from petal fall through cover sprays. Thiophanate-methyl or Pyraclostrobin for targeted bitter rot protection.
apple_anthracnose.ipm_recommendations: Scout cankers in early spring. Cover sprays should be timed based on cumulative rain events in the 6 weeks leading to harvest.

groundnut_tikka_disease.name: Groundnut Tikka (Cercospora Leaf Spot)
groundnut_tikka_disease.scientific_name: Cercospora arachidicola (Early leaf spot) & Phaeoisariopsis personata (Late leaf spot)
groundnut_tikka_disease.symptoms: Early leaf spot: circular reddish-brown to black spots with conspicuous yellow halos on upper leaf surface. Late leaf spot: smaller, darker carbon-black circular spots without yellow halos, with heavy black sporulation on the underside. Severe defoliation occurs, resulting in premature peg breakdown and shriveled pods.
groundnut_tikka_disease.causes_biology: Fungus perpetuates on crop residue, peanut shells, and volunteer seedlings in the field.
groundnut_tikka_disease.encouraging_conditions: Warm days (25°C to 30°C) with prolonged relative humidity (>80%) and persistent canopy dew periods.
groundnut_tikka_disease.spread_mechanism: Conidia are easily dislodged by wind, insects, and raindrops.
groundnut_tikka_disease.prevention_methods: Crop rotation with non-legumes (sorghum, pearl millet, maize). Seed dressing with Carbendazim (2 g/kg seed) or Thiram (3 g/kg).
groundnut_tikka_disease.cultural_control: Prompt destruction of crop residue after harvest. Intercropping groundnut with pearl millet or pigeon pea (4:1 ratio) to reduce disease spread rate.
groundnut_tikka_disease.biological_control: Spray neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) or Pseudomonas fluorescens (0.2%) at 40 and 55 days after sowing.
groundnut_tikka_disease.chemical_management: Mancozeb 75 WP (1 kg/ha) + Carbendazim 50 WP (500 g/ha) or Hexaconazole 5% EC (2 ml/L) or Chlorothalonil 75 WP (2 g/L).
groundnut_tikka_disease.ipm_recommendations: Initiate first protective spray when 1-2 spots per plant are observed at 35-40 days after sowing.

sugarcane_red_rot.name: Sugarcane Red Rot
sugarcane_red_rot.affected_parts: Stalk, vascular bundles, leaf midrib, and root crown
sugarcane_red_rot.symptoms: Canes show yellowing and drying of the third or fourth leaf from crown downwards, followed by total crown wilting. Split-open infected stalks show longitudinal reddening of internal pith tissue interrupted by distinct transverse white patches ('cross-wise white bands'). Fermented alcohol odor ('sour molasses') emits from rotting stalks.
sugarcane_red_rot.causes_biology: Soilborne and sett-borne fungus that colonizes nodal nodal buds and leaf scars.
sugarcane_red_rot.encouraging_conditions: Waterlogging, poor field drainage, continuous ratooning, warm temperatures (28°C to 32°C), and unseasonal water stress followed by heavy flooding.
sugarcane_red_rot.spread_mechanism: Infected seed setts are the primary source; irrigation runoff and floodwaters disperse conidia between fields.
sugarcane_red_rot.prevention_methods: Select setts strictly from certified disease-free nurseries. Moist hot water treatment (MHAT) of setts at 54°C for 2.5 hours or aerated steam therapy at 50°C. Plant red-rot resistant clones (e.g., Co 0238, Co 86032).
sugarcane_red_rot.cultural_control: Ensure rapid drainage of excess field water. Practice field sanitation and crop rotation with paddy or green manure crops. Avoid ratooning of infected crops.
sugarcane_red_rot.biological_control: Sett dip treatment with Trichoderma viride or T. harzianum (10 g/L) and soil application enriched with farmyard manure (2.5 kg Trichoderma in 250 kg FYM/ha).
sugarcane_red_rot.chemical_management: Sett dip in Carbendazim 50% WP (1 g/L) or Thiophanate methyl (1 g/L) for 15-20 minutes before planting. Chemical sprays have negligible effect once stalks are colonized.
sugarcane_red_rot.ipm_recommendations: Roguing of infected clumps along with root systems, followed by dusting the empty pit with bleaching powder.

rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.name: Rice Bacterial Leaf Blight (BLB)
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked translucent stripes starting at the leaf margins near the tips, turning grayish-white or straw-colored with wavy or undulated margins. On young seedlings (1-3 weeks post-transplanting), systemic infection causes rapid wilting and collapse of the entire tiller ('Kresek' or seedling wilt). Bacterial exudate ooze (milky droplets) dries into small amber spherical beads on leaf surfaces in early morning.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.causes_biology: Aerobic rod-shaped Gram-negative bacterium. Enters the rice plant through natural hydathodes at leaf margins or mechanical wounds caused by wind friction or handling during transplanting.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.encouraging_conditions: High temperatures (25°C to 34°C) coupled with high relative humidity (>85%). Severe tropical cyclones, torrential downpours, flooded paddies, and excessive nitrogen application.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.spread_mechanism: Bacteria are splashed by rain, carried through irrigation and floodwaters, and swept by windstorms.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.prevention_methods: Grow resistant rice cultivars containing Xa-resistance genes (e.g., Xa21, xa13, xa5). Treat seeds with Agrimycin-100 (0.05%) + Copper oxychloride (0.2%).
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.cultural_control: Drain fields periodically to aerate soil. Strictly regulate chemical nitrogen application; split into 3-4 doses with enhanced potash application. Remove weed hosts (Leersia grass) along field bunds.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.biological_control: Foliar spray of fresh cow dung slurry supernatant (20%) which harbors antagonistic bacterial competitors. Spray Pseudomonas fluorescens (2.5 kg/ha).
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.chemical_management: Copper Oxychloride 50 WP (2.5 g/L) combined with Streptocycline (streptomycin sulfate + tetracycline at 1 g / 10 L water). Apply at first sign of marginal blighting.
rice_bacterial_leaf_blight.ipm_recommendations: Cease top-dressing nitrogen immediately upon detecting lesions. Drain standing water to 2-3 cm depth during an active epidemic.

tomato_bacterial_spot.name: Tomato Bacterial Spot
tomato_bacterial_spot.scientific_name: Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria (syn. Xanthomonas perforans)
tomato_bacterial_spot.affected_parts: Leaves, stems, flower pedicels, calyx, and green fruits
tomato_bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, angular to circular dark greasy water-soaked spots (1-3 mm wide) on leaves, often surrounded by yellow halos. The centers of old leaf spots dry out and tear, creating a ragged shot-hole appearance. On green fruit, small blister-like scabby spots appear with raised brown roughened centers.
tomato_bacterial_spot.causes_biology: Seed-borne Gram-negative bacterium that overwinters on contaminated seeds, crop residue, and solanaceous weeds.
tomato_bacterial_spot.encouraging_conditions: Warm temperatures (24°C to 30°C) with persistent driving rain, fog, and prolonged leaf wetness periods.
tomato_bacterial_spot.spread_mechanism: Disseminated by driving rain, overhead irrigation, workers handling wet plants, and infested seeds.
tomato_bacterial_spot.prevention_methods: Use hot water seed treatment (50°C for 25 minutes for tomato seeds) or soak in 1.3% sodium hypochlorite for 1 minute. Rotate fields away from solanaceous crops for at least 2 years.
tomato_bacterial_spot.cultural_control: Switch to drip irrigation. Do not enter tomato fields while foliage is damp with dew or rain. Destroy volunteer plants.
tomato_bacterial_spot.biological_control: Bacteriophage biopesticides (AgriPhage) applied in the late afternoon to avoid UV inactivation. Bacillus amyloliquefaciens foliar sprays.
tomato_bacterial_spot.chemical_management: Preventative fixed copper formulations (Copper hydroxide 2.0 g/L) tank-mixed with Mancozeb (2.0 g/L) to combat copper-tolerant bacterial strains. Kasugamycin 3% SL (1.5 ml/L).
tomato_bacterial_spot.ipm_recommendations: Begin applications at seedling stage in greenhouses and continue every 7 to 10 days during rainy field periods.

cotton_bacterial_blight.name: Cotton Bacterial Blight / Black Arm
cotton_bacterial_blight.affected_parts: Cotyledons, leaves (angular leaf spot), branches (black arm), and bolls
cotton_bacterial_blight.symptoms: Four distinct diagnostic phases: 1) Water-soaked angular leaf spots bound by veinlets. 2) Vein blight where lesions travel along main veins. 3) 'Black Arm' phase where dark elongated girdling cankers develop on main stems and branches, causing breakage. 4) Boll rot where circular water-soaked sunken dark lesions ruin developing lint.
cotton_bacterial_blight.causes_biology: Bacteria survive in fuzzy seed lint, internal seed embryos, and dry crop residue left on soil surface.
cotton_bacterial_blight.encouraging_conditions: High humidity (85-90%) and warm ambient temperatures (30°C to 35°C), often triggered by heavy monsoon rains and sand-blasting winds.
cotton_bacterial_blight.spread_mechanism: Windblown rain splash, contaminated cultivators, and primary seed transmission.
cotton_bacterial_blight.prevention_methods: Acid delinting of cotton seeds with concentrated sulfuric acid (100 ml/kg seed) destroys seed-coat bacteria. Cultivate immune/resistant varieties.
cotton_bacterial_blight.cultural_control: Deep summer plowing to bury cotton stalks and infected debris. Thinning stands to improve row ventilation. Avoid excessive furrow flooding.
cotton_bacterial_blight.biological_control: Seed bacterization with Pseudomonas fluorescens (10 g/kg) and foliar spray at 0.2% concentration.
cotton_bacterial_blight.chemical_management: Copper oxychloride (2.5 g/L) + Streptocycline (1 g/10 L water) sprayed twice at 15-day intervals starting at early square formation.
cotton_bacterial_blight.ipm_recommendations: Eradicate alternate malvaceous weeds (Abutilon indicum). Scout for cotyledonary spots 2 weeks after emergence.

tomato_mosaic_virus.name: Tomato Mosaic & Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
tomato_mosaic_virus.scientific_name: Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV) / Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV)
tomato_mosaic_virus.affected_parts: Entire canopy, leaves, shoots, and fruit
tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Foliage exhibits prominent light and dark green mosaic mottling, leaf distortion, blister-like puckering, and 'shoestring' narrowing of leaflets. Plants infected early with TYLCV show severe stunting, erect bunchy growth habit, and upward curling of leaflet margins with chlorosis. Blossoms drop prematurely; fruits show uneven ripening with internal brown necrotic streaking.
tomato_mosaic_virus.causes_biology: ToMV is an exceptionally stable rod-shaped single-stranded RNA tobamovirus transmitted mechanically. TYLCV is a circular single-stranded DNA begomovirus transmitted persistently by the whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
tomato_mosaic_virus.encouraging_conditions: Dry, hot conditions that favor exponential whitefly population surges (temperatures >28°C). Greenhouses and nurseries with continuous cultivation cycles.
tomato_mosaic_virus.spread_mechanism: TYLCV: exclusively insect vectored by Bemisia tabaci biotypes. ToMV: highly infectious mechanical contact through workers' hands, clothes, trellising tools, and tobacco smoke residues.
tomato_mosaic_virus.prevention_methods: Plant TYLCV-resistant cultivars harboring Ty-1, Ty-2, or Ty-3 resistance genes. Use insect-proof 50-mesh nursery netting to produce virus-free transplants. Wash hands and tools with 10% trisodium phosphate (TSP) or skim milk before handling plants.
tomato_mosaic_virus.cultural_control: Install yellow sticky traps (30-40 traps/hectare) to monitor and mass-trap whitefly vectors. Rogue out and bag infected plants immediately upon symptom appearance.
tomato_mosaic_virus.biological_control: Conserve or release whitefly parasitoids Encarsia formosa or predatory bugs Macrolophus pygmaeus. Spraying azadirachtin (neem extract 10,000 ppm at 1.5 ml/L).
tomato_mosaic_virus.chemical_management: Viruses have no direct chemical cure. Management focuses on whitefly vector control: Imidacloprid 17.8% SL (0.5 ml/L) or Spiromesifen 22.9% SC (1 ml/L) or Dinotefuran 20% SG or Cyantraniliprole.
tomato_mosaic_virus.ipm_recommendations: Maintain a strict 2-month host-free crop break between solanaceous plantings. Eradicate weed reservoirs (nightshade, datura) along farm borders.

aphids_infestation.name: Cotton & Green Peach Aphids
aphids_infestation.affected_parts: Tender shoot tips, underside of leaves, flower buds
aphids_infestation.symptoms: Dense colonies of tiny pear-shaped soft-bodied insects (green, yellow, or black) clustered on terminal shoots and leaf undersides. Leaves cup downwards, wrinkle, turn yellow, and wither. Copious secretion of sticky sugary excreta ('honeydew') covers foliage, promoting dense growth of black sooty mold fungus that blocks photosynthesis. Vector for devastating plant viruses (PVY, CMV).
aphids_infestation.causes_biology: Parthenogenetic viviparous reproduction: adult wingless females give birth directly to live nymphs without mating, producing up to 10-15 generations per season. Winged forms (alatae) develop under crowding or host plant decline to colonize new fields.
aphids_infestation.encouraging_conditions: Mild, dry temperatures between 18°C and 26°C with moderate humidity. Excessive chemical nitrogen fertilizers that produce lush, succulent succulent foliage.
aphids_infestation.spread_mechanism: Alate (winged) aphids migrate on low-level wind currents across vast agricultural distances.
aphids_infestation.prevention_methods: Use reflective silver plastic mulches that disorient incoming winged aphids. Conserve natural field borders with flowering plants (coriander, fennel, mustard) to sustain beneficial predators.
aphids_infestation.cultural_control: Avoid excessive nitrogen top-dressing. High-pressure water spraying to physically knock colonies off home garden plants. Clip out heavily infested terminal branches.
aphids_infestation.biological_control: Key natural enemies: Ladybird beetles (Coccinella septempunctata), green lacewings (Chrysoperla carnea), syrphid fly larvae, and parasitoid wasps (Aphidius colemani). Entomopathogenic fungus: Verticillium lecanii (Beauveria bassiana at 5 g/L).
aphids_infestation.chemical_management: Threshold: 10% infested plants or 20 aphids/leaf. Soft chemistry: Insecticidal potassium salts of fatty acids (2%) or cold-pressed Neem oil (3-5 ml/L). Systemics: Flonicamid 50% WG (0.3 g/L), Acetamiprid 20% SP (0.2 g/L), or Thiamethoxam 25% WG (0.25 g/L).
aphids_infestation.ipm_recommendations: Preserve predatory ladybugs; avoid broad-spectrum pyrethroids that trigger catastrophic secondary aphid flare-ups by eliminating natural predators.

fall_armyworm.name: Fall Armyworm (FAW)
fall_armyworm.affected_parts: Leaf whorls, tassels, developing maize ears and cobs
fall_armyworm.symptoms: Young larvae scrape leaf epidermis creating 'window-pane' translucent patches. Older larvae bore deep into the central plant whorl, consuming growing tips and leaving large ragged holes in unfurling leaves ('shotgun damage'). Deep whorls become packed with abundant coarse moist sawdust-like fecal frass. Tassels and ears are penetrated, causing extensive ear rot.
fall_armyworm.causes_biology: Females lay 1000-2000 eggs in felt-like hairy masses on leaves. Larvae progress through 6 instars characterized by an inverted white 'Y' mark on the dark head capsule and four elevated black pinacula spots forming a square on the 8th abdominal segment. Pupation occurs underground in an earthen cocoon.
fall_armyworm.encouraging_conditions: Warm climates (24°C to 30°C). Drought conditions followed by intermittent rains. Continuous maize cropping without off-season breaks.
fall_armyworm.spread_mechanism: Adult moths are powerful nocturnal flyers, capable of migrating up to 500 km per generation on jet stream winds.
fall_armyworm.prevention_methods: Synchronized community planting to avoid overlapping vulnerable crop stages. Intercropping maize with non-hosts like Desmodium (push-pull strategy) or cowpea. Seed treatment with Cyantraniliprole or Chlorantraniliprole.
fall_armyworm.cultural_control: Deep summer plowing exposes underground pupae to predatory birds and desiccation. Handpicking egg masses and crushing early instars. Placing dry fine sand or wood ash into whorls to suffocate young larvae.
fall_armyworm.biological_control: Egg parasitoids: Trichogramma pretiosum or Telenomus remus (release 100,000 wasps/ha). Biopesticides: Bacillus thuringiensis kurstaki (Bt at 2 g/L), Spodoptera frugiperda Multiple Nucleopolyhedrovirus (SfMNPV at 1.5 ml/L), or Metarhizium rileyi.
fall_armyworm.chemical_management: Threshold: 5% infested whorls at seedling stage, 10-20% at mid-whorl stage. Directed spray right into the whorl: Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC (0.4 ml/L or 150 ml/ha) or Emamectin benzoate 5% SG (0.4 g/L) or Spinetoram 11.7% SC (0.5 ml/L).
fall_armyworm.ipm_recommendations: Deploy FAW sex pheromone delta traps (5 traps/ha) for early detection. Direct insecticide nozzles downwards straight into the funnel whorl where larvae hide.

whiteflies_infestation.name: Whiteflies
whiteflies_infestation.symptoms: Clouds of tiny (1 mm) moth-like white insects flutter vigorously when infested plants are disturbed. Foliage displays chlorotic speckling, silvering of leaf veins, and premature leaf drop. Nymphs excrete copious honeydew leading to extensive sooty mold colonization. Serves as primary vector for over 100 destructive geminiviruses including Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl and Cotton Leaf Curl Virus.
whiteflies_infestation.causes_biology: Oval yellowish eggs laid upright on slender stalks on leaf undersides. Flat translucent scale-like nymphs (crawlers and sessile instars) suck sap continuously.
whiteflies_infestation.encouraging_conditions: Hot, dry, and rainless weather (30°C to 38°C) with low relative humidity. Indiscriminate use of synthetic pyrethroids which eliminates predatory bugs.
whiteflies_infestation.spread_mechanism: Weak fliers over short distances, but transported hundreds of kilometers by atmospheric wind drafts and commercial seedling transport.
whiteflies_infestation.prevention_methods: Grow border barrier crops (2-3 rows of pearl millet, maize, or sorghum) around cotton and tomato plots. Install 40-50 yellow sticky cards per hectare for mass trapping. Use silver reflective plastic mulches.
whiteflies_infestation.cultural_control: Maintain strict weed control, targeting wild host weeds like Abutilon and Trianthema. Avoid nitrogen over-application.
whiteflies_infestation.biological_control: Parasitoid wasps: Encarsia formosa and Eretmocerus mundus. Predatory mirid bugs: Nesidiocoris tenuis and predatory mites: Amblyseius swirskii. Entomopathogenic sprays of Beauveria bassiana or Lecanicillium lecanii (5 g/L).
whiteflies_infestation.chemical_management: Economic threshold: 6-8 adults/leaf. Insect Growth Regulators (IGR): Pyriproxyfen 10% EC (1.5-2.0 ml/L) or Buprofezin 25% SC (1.5 ml/L). Systemics: Diafenthiuron 50% WP (1.2 g/L), Spiromesifen 22.9% SC (1 ml/L), or Afidopyropen 50 g/L DC.
whiteflies_infestation.ipm_recommendations: Target nymph stages with IGRs rather than relying on adulticides. Alternate chemistries between generation cycles to combat extreme insecticide resistance.

stem_borer.name: Yellow Rice Stem Borer
stem_borer.symptoms: At vegetative stage: larva bores inside the stem, severing vascular tissues at the base, causing central whorl leaf to roll, dry up, and die, known as 'Dead Heart' (easily pulled out with rotten odor). At reproductive stage: feeding severs the emerging panicle, resulting in unfilled, erect, completely white, bleached empty panicles termed 'Whiteheads'.
stem_borer.causes_biology: Moth lays disc-shaped egg clusters covered with brown anal hairs on tip of leaves. Larvae migrate to base of plant, penetrate leaf sheath, enter stem internodes, and pupate inside the straw.
stem_borer.encouraging_conditions: High nitrogen application, close plant spacing, warm humid conditions (25°C to 30°C), and low nocturnal temperatures during panicle initiation.
stem_borer.spread_mechanism: Adult female moths fly nocturnal flights toward light sources and oviposit on rice foliage.
stem_borer.prevention_methods: Clip seedling leaf tips before transplanting to destroy egg masses. Avoid excess seedling age; plant synchronously across contiguous basins. Drain fields at tillering to reduce borer emergence.
stem_borer.cultural_control: Harvest rice at ground level to destroy larvae overwintering in stubbles. Plowing and submerging stubbles immediately after harvest.
stem_borer.biological_control: Release egg parasitoid Trichogramma japonicum @ 100,000 wasps/ha at weekly intervals starting 30 days after transplanting. Conserve spiders (Lycosa pseudoannulata) and dragonflies.
stem_borer.chemical_management: Economic threshold: 2 egg masses/sq.m or 5% dead hearts or 1% whiteheads. Granular soil applications: Cartap hydrochloride 4% G (18-20 kg/ha) or Chlorantraniliprole 0.4% G (10 kg/ha). Foliar spray: Flubendiamide 39.35% SC (0.2 ml/L) or Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC (0.3 ml/L).
stem_borer.ipm_recommendations: Install light traps and pheromone traps (5-8 traps/ha) containing lure 'Scirpolure' to monitor moth surges and time parasitoid releases.

cotton_bollworm.name: Cotton / American Bollworm (Corn Earworm)
cotton_bollworm.affected_parts: Squares, flower buds, bolls, and green tomato fruits
cotton_bollworm.symptoms: Young larvae feed on tender leaves; older larvae bore into squares and bolls, leaving large circular entry holes with frass accumulated around edges. Typically feeds with only its head thrust inside the fruit or boll while the rest of the body remains outside. Attacked squares flare open ('flared squares') and shed prematurely. In tomatoes, causes deep rot holes.
cotton_bollworm.causes_biology: Spherical yellowish-white eggs laid singly on tender leaves and flowers. Larval color varies widely from greenish to brown with lateral wavy yellowish-white stripes.
cotton_bollworm.encouraging_conditions: Warm sunny weather following cloudiness and rainfall. Abundance of sequential host crops (chickpea, tomato, cotton).
cotton_bollworm.spread_mechanism: Highly mobile adult moths migrate over long distances (>200 km) guided by pheromones and host odors.
cotton_bollworm.prevention_methods: Plant trap crops: African marigold (1 row for every 14-16 rows of tomato) or castor/okra around cotton. Grow Bt-cotton hybrids containing Cry toxins.
cotton_bollworm.cultural_control: Handpick and destroy large caterpillars and flared squares. Deep summer plowing to expose pupae to scorching sun and birds. Install bird perches (T-shaped bamboo pegs @ 40-50/ha).
cotton_bollworm.biological_control: Release Trichogramma chilonis @ 150,000/ha. Spray Helicoverpa armigera Nucleopolyhedrovirus (HaNPV @ 250-500 LE/ha) in evening. Beauveria bassiana or Bt kurstaki (2 g/L).
cotton_bollworm.chemical_management: Economic threshold: 1 larva per plant or 5-10% damage to squares/bolls. Spray Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC (0.3 ml/L) or Spinosad 45% SC (0.3 ml/L) or Indoxacarb 14.5% SC (1.0 ml/L) or Emamectin benzoate 5% SG (0.4 g/L).
cotton_bollworm.ipm_recommendations: Rotate chemistries with differing modes of action (e.g. diamides, spinosyns, oxadiazines) to prevent resistance build-up.

thrips_infestation.name: Chilli & Onion Thrips
thrips_infestation.symptoms: Microscopic slender insects with fringed wings rasp tender foliage and suck oozing sap. Leaves curl upwards ('boat-shaped leaf curling'), develop silvery or bronze sheen on undersides, and leaf margins turn brittle. In peppers, leaves become stunted into 'murda' condition. On grape berries, rasping causes circular corky scarring around the pedicel (ring scarring). Vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus (TSWV).
thrips_infestation.causes_biology: Slender microscopic insects reproducing sexually or parthenogenetically. Eggs inserted inside leaf tissue; pupation occurs in soil litter.
thrips_infestation.encouraging_conditions: Hot, dry weather with intermittent periods of sunlight. Drought stress severely exacerbates plant susceptibility.
thrips_infestation.spread_mechanism: Carried passively by wind currents across crop canopies.
thrips_infestation.prevention_methods: Install blue sticky traps (30-40 traps/ha), which are more attractive to thrips than yellow traps. Intercropping chilli with maize or sorghum as wind barriers.
thrips_infestation.cultural_control: Overhead sprinkler irrigation physically washes thrips off leaf surfaces and destroys pupating soil stages. Deep irrigation reduces thermal stress.
thrips_infestation.biological_control: Predatory mites (Amblyseius swirskii, Neoseiulus cucumeris) and pirate bugs (Orius insidiosus). Foliar sprays of Entomopathogenic Lecanicillium lecanii (5 g/L) or 2% Pongamia oil.
thrips_infestation.chemical_management: Economic threshold: 2-3 thrips/leaf. Fipronil 5% SC (1.5-2.0 ml/L) or Spinetoram 11.7% SC (0.8 ml/L) or Cyantraniliprole 10.26% OD (1.2 ml/L) or Acetamiprid 20% SP (0.3 g/L).
thrips_infestation.ipm_recommendations: Never wait until severe leaf upward curling develops; scout leaf undersides with a 10x hand lens at early flowering.

leaf_miners.name: Serpentine Leaf Miner
leaf_miners.symptoms: Prominent whitish, winding, serpentine or zigzag mine trails etched through leaf mesophyll tissue. Larvae feed between upper and lower epidermis, leaving dark frass trails along mine margins. Heavily mined leaves turn brown, dry up prematurely, and drop, exposing developing fruits to sunscald.
leaf_miners.causes_biology: Tiny yellow and black fly lays eggs beneath leaf epidermis. Maggot hatches and feeds inside leaf parenchyma, emerging to pupate on the leaf surface or drop to the soil.
leaf_miners.encouraging_conditions: Warm temperatures (22°C to 28°C) and sheltered greenhouse environments.
leaf_miners.spread_mechanism: Adult flies fly locally; long-range transport occurs via infested transplant flats.
leaf_miners.prevention_methods: Use insect netting on nursery vents. Inspect transplants for feeding puncture dots before setting out in fields.
leaf_miners.cultural_control: Pick and hand-crush mined leaves early in the infestation. Clean cultivate weeds belonging to Solanaceae and Asteraceae.
leaf_miners.biological_control: Parasitoid wasps: Diglyphus isaea and Dacnusa sibirica provide up to 90% natural control. Neem seed kernel extract (NSKE 5%) or Azadirachtin (1%).
leaf_miners.chemical_management: Cyromazine 75% WP (0.5 g/L insect growth regulator specific to dipterous leaf miners) or Abamectin 1.9% EC (0.5 ml/L) with penetrating horticultural oil.
leaf_miners.ipm_recommendations: Avoid harsh pyrethroid sprays which slaughter Diglyphus wasps and trigger massive leafminer outbreaks.

rice_healthy.name: Rice (Healthy)
rice_healthy.symptoms: Uniform vibrant emerald green foliage with erect, clean leaf blades. No water-soaked streaks, diamond spindle lesions, or necrotic margins. Tillers are sturdy with clean nodes. Panicles emerge cleanly with full golden grain filling.
rice_healthy.causes_biology: Optimal agronomic health, balanced nutrient management, robust cellular vigor, and active systemic resistance.
rice_healthy.encouraging_conditions: Balanced soil fertility, appropriate water regimen (intermittent wetting and drying), and proper microclimatic spacing.
rice_healthy.prevention_methods: Continue proactive IPM monitoring, maintain 5 cm water level during tillering and panicle development, and apply balanced split nitrogen top-dressing.
rice_healthy.cultural_control: Weed manually or mechanically at 20 and 40 DAT. Maintain clean field bunds.
rice_healthy.biological_control: Encourage natural predatory spiders, mirid bugs, and Trichogramma wasps.
rice_healthy.chemical_management: No chemical intervention needed. Avoid unnecessary prophylactic fungicide sprays.
rice_healthy.ipm_recommendations: Regular weekly field scouting following standard agro-ecosystem analysis (AESA) protocols.

tomato_healthy.name: Tomato (Healthy)
tomato_healthy.symptoms: Foliage is deep green, crisp, and robust with no chlorotic spots, concentric target rings, or viral leaf curling. Stems are solid, upright, and free from cankers. Fruits develop smoothly without blossom-end rot or necrotic spots.
tomato_healthy.causes_biology: Healthy photosynthetic machinery with optimal root uptake of water and micronutrients.
tomato_healthy.encouraging_conditions: Even drip irrigation, well-drained loamy soil (pH 6.0-6.8), and good canopy ventilation.
tomato_healthy.prevention_methods: Maintain mulching to suppress soil splashes, stake plants securely, and remove bottom suckers touching soil.
tomato_healthy.cultural_control: Irrigate consistently to prevent calcium-related blossom-end rot. Avoid overhead sprinklers.
tomato_healthy.biological_control: Maintain flowering companion borders (marigold, basil) to attract beneficial pollinators and predators.
tomato_healthy.ipm_recommendations: Continue bi-weekly visual inspections of upper and lower leaf surfaces.

potato_healthy.name: Potato (Healthy)
potato_healthy.symptoms: Vigorous dense canopy with rich dark green leaves free of water-soaked lesions, target rings, or aphid clusters. Stems are thick and erect; tubers beneath soil show smooth skin without necrotic rot rings.
potato_healthy.causes_biology: Optimal seed vitality, uninfected tuber propagation, and well-balanced soil fertilization.
potato_healthy.encouraging_conditions: Cool temperate weather (15°C to 22°C), well-hilled friable soil, and timely drip irrigation.
potato_healthy.prevention_methods: Ensure continuous adequate soil hilling to prevent tuber greening and late blight zoospore penetration.
potato_healthy.cultural_control: Maintain adequate moisture during tuber initiation; scout fields regularly for early blight signs.
potato_healthy.biological_control: Encourage native ground beetles and ladybugs.
potato_healthy.ipm_recommendations: Keep weather stations checked for late blight risk indices (Simphyt/Blitecast).

maize_healthy.name: Maize / Corn (Healthy)
maize_healthy.symptoms: Thick, dark-green arched leaves with smooth margins and no shotgun holes, window-paning frass, or rust pustules. Central whorl is clean and intact; ears develop full tip-fill with golden silks.
maize_healthy.causes_biology: Optimum physiological performance and genetic vigor.
maize_healthy.encouraging_conditions: Warm sunny days, adequate soil nitrogen, and well-aerated soil.
maize_healthy.prevention_methods: Scout central whorls for early fall armyworm egg masses. Maintain balanced N-P-K fertilization.
maize_healthy.cultural_control: Intercrop with pulses; practice crop rotation with legumes.
maize_healthy.biological_control: Conserve predatory earwigs, assassin bugs, and spiders.
maize_healthy.ipm_recommendations: Maintain pheromone traps for early moth influx warnings.

cotton_healthy.name: Cotton (Healthy)
cotton_healthy.symptoms: Deep green palmate leaves free from angular greasy spots, aphid honeydew, or curled margins. Squares and young bolls are clean, plump, and firmly attached without larval bore holes or flaring.
cotton_healthy.causes_biology: Robust vegetative and reproductive balance in healthy soil.
cotton_healthy.encouraging_conditions: Warm sunny climate (25°C to 35°C), adequate furrow or drip irrigation, and timely weed suppression.
cotton_healthy.prevention_methods: Regular scouting of terminal shoots and lower leaf surfaces for sucking pests.
cotton_healthy.cultural_control: Maintain border trap crops (castor, marigold) to intercept bollworms.
cotton_healthy.biological_control: Protect green lacewings and predatory geocorid bugs.
cotton_healthy.ipm_recommendations: Track square retention percentage; healthy crops retain >75% of early squares.

grape_healthy.name: Grape (Healthy)
grape_healthy.symptoms: Broad, lustrous green leaves without oil spots, powdery powdery patches, or thrips ring scarring. Clusters display uniform berry development with natural waxy bloom and zero fruit splitting.
grape_healthy.causes_biology: Balanced vine balance, open canopy structure, and optimal root vigor.
grape_healthy.encouraging_conditions: Adequate sunlight penetration, good air circulation, and controlled deficit irrigation post-veraison.
grape_healthy.prevention_methods: Continue shoot positioning and selective leaf removal in the fruiting zone to maximize solar exposure.
grape_healthy.cultural_control: Keep cover crops mowed; avoid over-vigorous cane growth.
grape_healthy.ipm_recommendations: Monitor degree-day accumulations for mildew and berry moth models.

unknown_unsupported.name: Unknown or Unsupported Image
unknown_unsupported.symptoms: The uploaded image does not contain identifiable crop foliage, recognizable pathology symptoms, or distinct pest characteristics supported by the model's trained classes. Features match non-agricultural objects, random backgrounds, extreme blur, or out-of-distribution input.
unknown_unsupported.causes_biology: The AI classifier evaluated the deep feature embeddings and determined that prediction entropy is high, and no agricultural class crossed the necessary 55% statistical confidence threshold.
unknown_unsupported.encouraging_conditions: Poor lighting, extreme camera motion blur, non-plant items (faces, animals, machinery), or crops not currently in the training registry.
unknown_unsupported.prevention_methods: Capture a close-up, sharp, well-illuminated photograph directly focusing on the affected leaf blade, fruit surface, stem lesion, or insect pest.
unknown_unsupported.cultural_control: Retake photo in natural daylight against a neutral background. Avoid extreme angles and high-glare reflections.
unknown_unsupported.chemical_management: DO NOT apply chemical treatments based on unverified or low-confidence identifications.
unknown_unsupported.ipm_recommendations: Submit the sample to an accredited local agricultural extension specialist or university plant diagnostic clinic.
